extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and scholars of science fiction (especially Frank Herbert/Dune) and writers interested in epic world-building
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and critical commentary useful for creating or evaluating epic science-fiction world-building, themes, and representation (using Frank Herbert's Dune as a primary example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered storytelling / 'layer technique'
rubrics_metrics.description: "I build on a layer technique, and of course putting in religion and religious ideas you can play one against the other." (Herbert quote)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple narrative threads (e.g., setting, religion, politics, ecology) layered together so they can be set in tension or used to illuminate one another. The page quotes Herbert describing intentionally combining desert atmosphere and religious ideas so different threads interact; treat layering as a deliberate compositional strategy rather than a single-thread story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic world-building: names and cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Referenced by the article "Epic World-Building: Names and Cultures in 'Dune'" (Names: A Journal of Onomastics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop distinct onomastics (names, naming systems) and cultural details to give an epic science-fiction setting depth and internal consistency. Use names and cultural practices to signal history, power structures, and relationships between peoples; scholarship on Dune is cited as a model for this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecology and climate as central speculative theme (climate fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Page cites pieces calling Dune a "climate fiction pioneer" and highlights the novel's ecological lessons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate environmental and ecological systems into speculative narratives so they shape plot, conflict, and world dynamics. Treat ecological change (desertification, resource dependency, etc.) as a driver of social and political consequences rather than mere backdrop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with Arabic/Islamic motifs and cultural source material
rubrics_metrics.description: References such as "Arabic and Islamic themes in Frank Herbert's Dune" and scholarly discussion of Orientalism in science fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on Arabic, Islamic, or other cultural motifs, be explicit about sources and intentions and attend to representation and critique (avoid unreflective exoticism/Orientalism). The page points to scholarship analyzing both inspiration and problematic appropriations in Dune's use of such motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women's agency and complex female characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites works like "Women's Agency in the Dune Universe: Tracing Women's Liberation through Science Fiction" and "Frank Herbert, the Bene Gesserit, and the Complexity of Women in the World of Dune."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or create female characters with attention to agency, institutional roles (e.g., Bene Gesserit), and complexity—not merely as plot devices. Scholarship cited examines how Herbert's work can be read in terms of women's liberation and complex power dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard science-fiction plausibility / scientific grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: References to "Hard Science Fiction" and discussion of readers of hard SF (e.g., James Gunn's piece).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For work aiming at a 'hard SF' audience, ensure scientific and technical elements are plausible, internally consistent, and influential on plot and world mechanics. The page positions Dune relative to expectations of scientific rigor and reader reception in hard SF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mythic/archetypal structures (monomyth/fractal pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites "The Monomyth as Fractal Pattern in Frank Herbert's Dune Novels" and related scholarship on mythic patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ archetypal and mythic narrative patterns (hero's journey, fractal/iterative uses of the monomyth) to give epic scale and resonance; consider layering, inversion, or fractal use of such patterns to create depth rather than straightforward imitation.
